scenes.vo: The Union Finance Minister and a minister from every State sit at one table, the GST Council. Guess first. Can the Centre alone push a decision through? Can all the States together outvote the Centre?

spec.title: Who decides GST: Delhi or the States?
spec.sub: GST and the rest, part two

scenes.vo: Hold your guess. First, why does this table exist at all?
This is part two of three. Part one was who really pays. This part is how the Constitution made one tax possible.

labels.text: OUR SUMMARY: excise and services with the Centre · sales with the States
ONE TAX ON THE WHOLE CHAIN?

scenes.vo: Before GST, the Constitution gave the Centre and the States separate tax powers. Roughly, before GST the Centre taxed manufacture through excise, and services; the States taxed the sale of goods. That is our summary of the entries the amendment later cut. So one tax on the whole supply chain did not fit into either list.

So Parliament amended the Constitution. The hundred and first Amendment Act received the President's assent on the eighth of September, twenty sixteen. Its GST Council article came into force on the twelfth of September. The other changes to the Constitution followed four days later.

labels.text: ART. 246A · Parliament and the States both
ART. 269A · collected by the Centre, shared

scenes.vo: The key new article is two hundred forty-six A. It gives both Parliament and the State legislatures the power to make GST laws. But when a supply crosses a State border, only Parliament can make the law. That inter-State tax is collected by the Centre and shared, under Article two hundred sixty-nine A.

labels.text: ART. 366(12A) · a tax on the supply of goods, services or both

scenes.vo: The Constitution also defines GST. It is any tax on the supply of goods, services or both. The one exception is alcohol for drinking. And services are defined simply as anything other than goods.
Old powers were cut back. The article for service tax was removed. The Centre's excise now covers only petrol, diesel, crude oil, natural gas, aviation fuel and tobacco products.

labels.text: from the Centre: excise · service tax · extra customs duty
from the States: VAT · CST · luxury · entry · entertainment …

scenes.vo: Into GST went a long list. From the Centre, central excise, service tax and the extra customs duty on imports. From the States, VAT, central sales tax, luxury tax, entry tax and entertainment tax, among others. The Finance Ministry counts seventeen taxes and thirteen cesses in all.

labels.text: with the Union Minister of State, revenue or finance
every State: its finance or taxation minister

scenes.vo: But who recommends the rates for this shared tax? Not Parliament alone, and not any one State. Article two hundred seventy-nine A creates the GST Council. The Union Finance Minister chairs it, with the Union Minister of State in charge of revenue or finance. Every State sends its finance or taxation minister, or another minister it nominates.

labels.text: the date for petrol, diesel and three other fuels
NCERT: One Nation, One Tax, One Market
the Constitution: a harmonised national market

scenes.vo: The Council recommends almost everything. Which taxes merge, which goods are taxed or exempt, the rates and the thresholds. It also recommends the date from which petrol, diesel and three other fuels enter GST. And it must aim for a harmonised national market. NCERT titles its GST box One Nation, One Tax, One Market. The Constitution's words are harmonised structure and harmonised national market.

labels.text: OUR WORKING: neither alone reaches it

scenes.vo: Now your guess. Every decision needs three-fourths of the weighted votes of members present and voting. The Centre's vote counts as one-third. All the States together count as two-thirds. Our working: one-third alone is short of three-fourths. Two-thirds alone is short too. So neither the Centre nor all the States can decide without the other.

labels.text: half the State legislatures must ratify
a way to settle Centre-State disputes

scenes.vo: The design has more locks. Changing the Council article needs ratification by at least half the State Legislatures, not just Parliament. The Council must also set up a way to settle disputes between the Centre and the States. And the Act promised the States compensation for five years, for any revenue they lost. That story is part three.

labels.text: 1 July 2017 · a midnight session of Parliament
NCERT: the biggest tax reform since Independence

scenes.vo: GST began at midnight, as the first of July twenty seventeen began, in a special midnight session of Parliament. NCERT calls it the biggest tax reform since Independence.

labels.text: Union of India v Mohit Minerals (2022)

scenes.vo: But is the Council's word law? A case about shipping settled it. Importers were charged IGST on the ocean freight paid by the foreign seller to a shipping line. In twenty twenty-two, the Supreme Court struck that levy down.

lines.text: The Union argued: recommendations must bind

scenes.vo: On the way, the Court answered the bigger question. The Union argued the Council's recommendations must bind Parliament and the States, or there would be an impasse. The Court disagreed. It held the recommendations are persuasive, not binding. One reason: Parliament dropped a proposed Article two hundred seventy-nine B. It was an authority to rule on departures from the Council's recommendations. The Court read that as meant to keep recommendations persuasive.

labels.text: rules under the CGST and IGST Acts: bound
Parliament and the States keep their power to make laws
equal power to legislate on GST

scenes.vo: But the Court drew a line. When the Government makes rules under the CGST and IGST Acts, it is bound by the Council's recommendations. Parliament and the State legislatures keep their own power to make laws. The Court described Indian federalism as a dialogue between cooperative and uncooperative federalism, from collaboration to contestation. It said the Union and the States have equal power to legislate on GST.

labels.text: each legislature keeps its law-making power

scenes.vo: So who decides GST, Delhi or the States? Our summary: at the Council, both together and neither alone. And each legislature keeps its own power to make GST laws.

lines.text: Art. 269A: inter-State tax, collected by the Centre and shared
Art. 279A Council: three-fourths vote; Centre one-third, States two-thirds
Mohit Minerals: persuasive, not binding · cooperative federalism

scenes.vo: For the exam, write it this way. The hundred and first Amendment gave Parliament and the States a shared power under two hundred forty-six A. Inter-State supply is taxed by the Centre and shared, under two hundred sixty-nine A. The Council under two hundred seventy-nine A recommends, with a three-fourths weighted vote, Centre one-third, States two-thirds. Mohit Minerals held its recommendations persuasive, not binding. The Court said GST aims at cooperative federalism, and called Indian federalism a dialogue between cooperative and uncooperative federalism.
Then came twenty twenty, and the promise of five years of compensation met a pandemic. That is part three.
